Plan Lab

Twenty-one experiments in rewriting a task plan as something you can run, fly over, play, zoom into, or read like a story, without dropping any detail. Every experiment renders the same two real plans. Each one is a single self-contained HTML file, and every AC, decision, guard rail or finding, phase and file stays reachable in it.

GREEN FIELD · #062

062 · auto-mail walking skeleton

A new auto mail subsystem. 12 inherited guard rails → 13 ACs, 9 decisions, 5 phases in a strict chain, 52 files (40 new), 8 review threads.

BROWN FIELD · #052

052 · reflect-tool hardening

Fixes 9 findings (F1–F11) in the existing auto reflect. 9 decisions, 14 ACs, 7 phases in a DAG, 37 files (27 edits, 1 delete), 6 review threads.

Batch 3 · legible trees

Redoes the favourites in the show-me style: plain monospace indented trees with a + − ~ ≠ gutter and a right-hand column for G/AC/D notes. These are prototypes of the proposed end state: goals as the landing view, then base→planned→built, a phase step-through, and a quiz on the fragile decisions with comment threads.

Batch 2 · blends

Combines the three favourites from batch 1 (01 play the journey, 10 test the reader, 11 overview + drill) with three new slices: file system (folders → files → symbols), dependency tree and call stack. All six read the same normalised model: ◎ G goals (5–8, one sentence each) → ✓ AC reproducible verification → ◆ D decisions. Symbols, imports, test names and call stacks come from the code as built.

Batch 1 · eleven directions

What the lab found

These are defects the experiments found in the final, reviewed plans, by computing from the plan data, running the spec or drawing it. None of them was caught by a review thread. Each one is a structured-data or consistency problem, and a plan linter could detect every one.

Green field vs brown field has a visual signature

Every experiment was asked to make the difference visible. The same shapes came up again and again.

Lessons for the next plan format

Across all eleven, the rich views were cheap wherever the plan carried structure and expensive wherever the agents had to extract it from prose.

1 · Declare links, don't narrate them

depends-on, files, phases and tests as attributes gave the critical path, file-conflict checks, traceability and coverage gaps with no extra work. Links that exist only in prose (for example "(F5/F7)" in file notes) had to be recovered by hand, so make them fields.

2 · One source for each fact

AC phases= and the Success Criteria list disagree for 9 ACs. Mermaid DAGs disagree with depends-on. Draw diagrams from the data rather than keeping a second copy.

3 · Make rejected alternatives items

Give each alternative its own ID, its reason, and the rails or ACs it would break. That is what powered the counterfactual mode in 04 and the matching puzzles in 10. Today it's buried in prose.

4 · Push review warnings to where the work happens

The most useful cautions live in resolved threads. Mission control (07) moved them onto the phase card. A plan should attach them to the phase or file they affect.

5 · Tag level of detail

Summary, key points and verbatim versions of each item let semantic zoom (02), the poster (09) and scrollytelling (03) choose a level instead of guessing.

6 · Pin the strings that matter

The simulator (01) had to borrow the nudge text, flag naming and error messages from shipped code. If a string is part of the contract, the plan should state it.

7 · Always keep a way back to the source

Every lossy format (comic, poster, story) was only trustworthy because of a one-click path to the verbatim text. Stable IDs on everything make that possible.

8 · Anchor to real repo state

Code city (06) and semantic zoom (02) used the git tree at plan time. A plan that records its base commit can show exactly what it's building on.
